metadata.description: Two foundational papers establishing the same compressed-sensing recovery guarantees from substantially different theoretical machinery. Candes-Tao (paper A) builds a Restricted Isometry Property / Restricted Orthogonality framework around constants $\delta_S, \theta_{S,S'}$ and proves exact $\ell_1$ recovery of S-sparse signals via dual-certificate construction. Donoho (paper B) builds a Gel'fand-width / CS1-CS3 framework controlling nullspace concentration $\nu(\Phi,J)$ and proves near-optimal $\ell_2$ approximation rates of compressible signals. The two papers tackle the same underlying problem (sparse recovery via $\ell_1$ minimization with random Gaussian / spherical sampling) using genuinely disjoint technical vocabularies; matches are mostly at the level of conceptual roles rather than exact mathematical objects, justifying the CF (competing frameworks) classification.

matches.explanation: Both define the $\ell_0$-minimization problem $(P_0)$: find the sparsest solution $\theta$ to a linear system. Same combinatorial NP-hard problem, identical names $(P_0)$ across both papers.

Both define Basis Pursuit / $(P_1)$: $\min \|\theta\|_1$ subject to a linear constraint, recast as an LP. Identical problem, identical name. Donoho cites Chen-Donoho-Saunders (1999) as origin; Candes-Tao re-derive it independently in the decoding context.

Candes-Tao's $(P'_1) = \min \|y - Ag\|_1$ is mathematically equivalent to Donoho's Basis Pursuit (paper A makes this equivalence explicit via the annihilator $F$ with $FA=0$). The two formulations are the dual sides of the same optimization but applied to different problem framings: A's is a decoding problem, B's is reconstruction from compressive measurements.

Both papers give the standard LP reformulation of $\ell_1$ minimization with slack variables. A's $\min 1^T t$ s.t. $-t \le y - Ag \le t$ and B's $\min 1^T z$ s.t. $Az = y_n, z\ge 0$ are the two textbook ways of linearizing $\|\cdot\|_1$; equivalent under change of variable.

Both papers' core algorithm is the LP that solves Basis Pursuit. A's 'LP decoder for $(P'_1)$' and B's 'Basis Pursuit (linear programming reconstruction)' are the same algorithm modulo the decoding vs reconstruction framing.

A's restricted isometry constants $\delta_S$ (the canonical RIP) and B's CS1-CS3 conditions both quantify how well a measurement matrix preserves geometry on sparse vectors. CS1 ($\sigma_{\min}(\Phi_J) > \eta_1$) is the lower-RIP-like piece. The conditions are not literally identical (Donoho deliberately splits the requirement into three pieces and works with column-norm form), but they play the same role and any RIP-good matrix obeys CS1-CS3 and vice versa for the regime considered. Famously DISJOINT vocabulary - the heart of the parallel-rediscovery / competing-frameworks split.

A's restricted orthogonality constants $\theta_{S,S'}$ control inner products between disjointly-supported sparse images. CS3 in Donoho ($Q_{J^c}(v) \ge \eta_3/\sqrt{\log(m/n)}\,\|v\|_1$ on $V_J$) plays a related role: bounding cross-action of $\Phi_J$ and $\Phi_{J^c}$. Conceptually the same incoherence-between-supports role, but encoded via a quotient-norm rather than an inner-product bilinear form.

A's Lemma (Unique sparse recovery from $\delta_{2S}<1$): RIP gives uniqueness of S-sparse representations. B's Theorem 8 ($\ell_1$/$\ell_0$ equivalence): under CS1-CS3 the unique $\ell_0$ solution coincides with the $\ell_1$ solution. Both connect a geometric matrix condition to uniqueness/identifiability of sparse solutions - A via the RIP-style invertibility argument, B via the nullspace concentration $\nu(\Phi,J) < 1/2$ argument.

A's main recovery theorem (Theorem 1.3): under $\delta_S+\theta_S+\theta_{S,2S}<1$, $\ell_1$ minimization exactly recovers any S-sparse vector. B's Theorem 8 gives exact $\ell_0$/$\ell_1$ recovery for sparse signals (matching A's exact-recovery claim) and Theorem 9 extends to compressible signals with stable rates. Same conclusion (correct recovery via $\ell_1$), different sufficient conditions (RIP/ROP vs CS1-CS3). The proofs are completely different: A via dual certificate built iteratively from Lemma 2.1; B via nullspace concentration and stability lemma.

A's decoding theorem 1.4 specializes Theorem 1.3 to the LP-decoding setup ($y = Af + e$ with sparse $e$). B's Theorem 8 is the CS-side $\ell_1/\ell_0$ equivalence. Both certify exact recovery in the noiseless / sparse-corruption case. The decoding framing is unique to A; the underlying mathematical content matches B's $\ell_0/\ell_1$ result.

Both papers prove that random matrices satisfy their respective sparse-recovery conditions with overwhelming probability, supplying the existence of usable measurement matrices. A: i.i.d. Gaussian $F$ obeys $\delta_S+\theta_S+\theta_{S,2S}<1$ for $r=S/m$ below an explicit numerical threshold. B: matrices with i.i.d. uniform-on-sphere columns obey CS1-CS3 with overwhelming probability ($P(\Omega_n^c) \le e^{-\beta n}$); 'ubiquity' theorem says generic matrices are CS matrices. Same 'random matrices work' theme, different distributions (Gaussian vs uniform on sphere; equivalent up to normalization) and different geometric quantities being controlled.

A's Lemma 3.1 is a uniform large-deviation bound on $\delta_S$ for Gaussian matrices via per-subset concentration + union bound + entropy ($\log\binom{m}{S} \approx mH(r)$). B decomposes the analogous task into a chain of lemmas: per-subset eigenvalue large-deviation (LP21.5), combining principle / union bound (LP21.6), per-subset $\epsilon$-isometry (LP21.8), spherical sections (LP21.7), assembled into LP21.4 controlling $\sigma_{\min}$ across all subsets. Same probabilistic technique (per-subset concentration + entropy union bound) at finer granularity in B.

Both proofs implement the union-bound-over-subsets argument with a Stirling/entropy estimate for $\binom{m}{S}$. A uses $\log\binom{m}{S} = mH(r) + O(\log m)$ exactly; B uses the cruder $\log\binom{m}{k} \le k\log m$. Same proof technique, slightly different bookkeeping.

Composite L2-vs-L1 entry. A's proof of Lemma 3.1 (PP2.6) decomposes into four steps (PSP2.18-21): reduce to $|T|=S$ via monotonicity, apply Ledoux concentration per subset, Stirling for $\log\binom{m}{S}$, balance exponent. B aggregates the same machinery into separate L1 lemmas: per-subset large-deviation (LP21.5), combining principle (LP21.6), and the proof of LP21.6 (PP21.10) which is the union-bound step. Match is on the level of the shared argument scheme (fixed-set concentration + union bound over subsets), with different granularities in the two extractions.

Both are cited concentration-of-measure ingredients providing per-subset eigenvalue/singular-value tail bounds. A cites Ledoux (Gaussian concentration giving $\sigma_{\max}(F_T), \sigma_{\min}(F_T)$ tails). B cites Donoho [11], Szarek for $\lambda_{\min}(\Phi_J^T\Phi_J)$ tail $\le e^{-n\beta}$. Same role (per-fixed-subset spectral large deviation); Donoho's version is for unit-sphere columns and Candes-Tao's is for Gaussian, but both are subgaussian-type concentration.

Marchenko-Pastur a.s. limits for extremal eigenvalues of $F_T^*F_T$ are cited only by Candes-Tao (used to obtain explicit numerical constants in the Gaussian threshold). Donoho works with unit-sphere columns and uses concentration tail bounds rather than the asymptotic Wishart spectrum, so this external is not in B.

A's dual sparse reconstruction property in $\ell_2$ form (Lemma 2.1) is the workhorse for A's iterative dual-certificate construction. B does not use a dual-certificate-via-$\ell_2$-iteration argument; instead B's $\ell_1$ recovery proof uses nullspace concentration $\nu(\Phi,J)$. There is a related but distinct sign-pattern embedding lemma (LP21.9, LP21.10) - see separate match - but those are NOT $\ell_2$ dual certificates in A's sense.

A's Lemma 2.2 produces a dual certificate $w$ with $\langle w, v_j\rangle = \sgn(c_j)$ on $T$ and $|\langle w, v_j\rangle|<1$ off $T$, exactly the dual feasibility condition for $(P_1)$. B's sign-pattern embedding lemmas (LP21.9 uniform, LP21.10 individual) construct, for each sign pattern $\sigma$, a $y$ with $|\langle\phi_i, y\rangle|\le 1$ for $i\notin J$ - same dual-feasibility object. The constructions differ (A: telescoping iteration of Lemma 2.1; B: iterative kill-and-project algorithm AP21.4), but both deliver the LP duality witness used in the recovery proof.

Composite proof-level match. A's proof of Lemma 2.2 (PP2.3) constructs the $\ell_\infty$ dual certificate by telescoping $w := \sum_n (-1)^{n-1} w_n$ from iterated applications of Lemma 2.1 with geometric-series convergence. B's proofs of the sign-pattern embedding lemmas (PP21.11 uniform via VC + union, PP21.12 individual via Gaussian large-deviations and event-chain telescoping) are entirely different technically but produce the analogous dual-feasibility witness. Both proofs use a recursive/telescoping reduction of the residual on an exceptional set.

Composite L1-cluster-of-L1 proofs. A's proof of Theorem 1.3 (PP2.4) is a one-shot duality argument: given a dual certificate from Lemma 2.2 with $\langle w, v_j\rangle = \sgn(c_j)$ on $T$ and $|\langle w, v_j\rangle|<1$ off $T$, comparing $\|d\|_1$ to $\|c\|_1$ via $w$ forces $d = c$. B's recovery proof is split: PP21.6 ($\ell_1/\ell_0$ equivalence via $\nu < 1/2$), PP21.8 (stability lemma), PP21.9 (top-$k$ truncation + width-to-$\ell_2$ conversion). Both prove the same recovery conclusion via the same overall logic (dual certificate / nullspace structure) but using disjoint technical vehicles.

Composite L2 step-block alignment for the main recovery proof. A's PSP2.12-15: existence of minimizer + dual certificate from Lemma 2.2 + $\|d\|_1$ bound via $w$ + force $d_j = 0$ off $T$. B's PSP21.10-13: choose $J$ as top-$\rho_0 n/\log m$ entries + bound truncation residual and $\nu(\Phi,J)$ + apply $\ell_1$ stability + convert $\ell_1$ bound to $\ell_2$ via width. Both proof DAGs implement the same high-level scheme (truncate to $J$, exploit $\Phi$-condition on $J$, conclude via duality / nullspace control), with disjoint local lemmas.

A's $\theta$-$\delta$ comparison lemma ($\theta_{S,S'} \le \delta_{S+S'} \le \theta_{S,S'}+\max(\delta_S,\delta_{S'})$) is internal to A's RIP/ROP framework. B has no $\theta$ analogue, so no comparison lemma exists; this is a paper-A-specific contribution.

A's sparsity-of-errors equation ($\|e\|_0 \le \rho m$) is a decoding-context object with no direct counterpart in B. B's analogous notion is the $\ell_p$-ball / weak-$\ell_p$ / 'compressibility class' (DP21.1, DP21.11), which encodes signal sparsity rather than error sparsity. The two play similar roles in their respective papers but in non-corresponding positions (signal vs noise).

The annihilator reduction $\tilde y = F(Af + e) = Fe$ is specific to A's decoding framing. B works directly with the measurement equation $y = \Phi\theta$ and never builds an annihilator; the decoding-to-compressed-sensing translation is implicit but not formalized in B.
Unit-norm characterization of $\delta_1$ is internal to A's RIP framework with no B counterpart.

A's sufficient-condition equation $\delta_S + \delta_{2S} + \delta_{3S} < \rho_{p/m}(r)$ is the explicit Gaussian-regime numerical bound. B does not produce an explicit closed-form numerical threshold of this kind - it states existence of constants $\eta_i, \rho$ without computing the optimal exponent.

Composite cluster: 'optimal recovery of compressible signals'. A's Theorem 5.1 + the supporting compressible-class definition $\mathcal{F}_s(B)$ + UUP/ERP definitions + remark RP2.2 establish that under RIP-type hypotheses, $\ell_1$ minimization gives near-optimal $\ell_2$ rates on power-law-decaying signals. B's Theorem 9 gives the very same rate $(n/\log m)^{1/2-1/p}$ for $0<p<1$ on $\ell_p$-balls, with the compressibility classes DP21.1 ($\ell_p$-ball) and DP21.11 (weak $\ell_p$-ball) corresponding to A's $\mathcal{F}_s(B)$ class. This is the most directly comparable result across the two papers, with matching exponents.

A's numerical experiments table (m=2n, m=4n recovery thresholds 17%, 34%) is empirical/example content. B's examples (Bump Algebra, BV, $C^2$ images) are theoretical illustrations of compression rates, not Monte Carlo experiments - different style of example.
A's open problem (improve the ~2% Gaussian threshold; finite-alphabet extensions) is paper-A specific. B does not list this as open work.
A's remark on possibly improving the $\delta_S+\theta_{S,S}+\theta_{S,2S}<1$ condition by a softer iterative-correction argument is internal RIP-framework speculation, with no B analogue.

A's 'linear code decoding problem' (recover $f$ from $y = Af + e$) and B's 'optimal recovery problem' (recover $x \in X$ from $I_n(x)$) are the high-level problems of the two papers. They are isomorphic under the annihilator reduction $\tilde y = Fe$ (A) and the CS measurement $y_n = \Phi\theta$ (B), but framed in different communities (coding theory vs information-based complexity / approximation theory).

B's 'information operator $I_n$' and the minimax errors $E_n(X), E_n^{\mathrm{Adapt}}(X)$ are IBC/Optimal-Recovery vocabulary specific to the Donoho framing. A does not introduce a minimax framework; it works with deterministic exact-recovery statements rather than worst-case error rates.

B's Gel'fand and Kolmogorov $n$-widths, the duality formula $d_n(b_{p,m};\ell_q)=d^n(b_{q',m};\ell_{p'})$, and the cited Kashin-Garnaev-Gluskin theorem are the heart of B's approximation-theory machinery. A makes no use of $n$-widths or KGG. This is exactly the famously DISJOINT vocabulary the v2 prompt warns about.

B's 'width relative to operator $w(\Phi,X)$' and the optimization $(Q_p)$ defining it are B-specific objects controlling the radius of the kernel section. No direct A counterpart - A controls the RIP constants $\delta_S, \theta_{S,S'}$ instead.
B's quotient norm $Q_{J^c}(v) = \min \|\theta\|_{\ell_1(J^c)}$ s.t. $\Phi_{J^c}\theta = v$ is internal to the CS3 condition. No A analogue.

B's nullspace concentration $\nu(\Phi,J)$ is the central quantity of B's recovery proof. A's proofs do not use a nullspace-concentration formulation; A controls things via dual certificates instead. The conceptual role overlaps with A's RIP+ROP combination but neither object is a direct match for $\nu$.

B's $\epsilon$-isometry between $\ell_2(J)$ and $\ell_1^n$ ($(1-\epsilon)\|\alpha\|_2 \le \sqrt{\pi/(2n)}\|\Phi_J\alpha\|_1 \le (1+\epsilon)\|\alpha\|_2$) is a CS2-type spherical-section condition. A's RIP is an $\ell_2 \to \ell_2$ isometry; the $\ell_2 \to \ell_1$ flavour is uniquely Donoho's.
B's tight-frame setup and the corresponding extension remark are B-specific; A works in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with no transform domain.

B's main rate theorem $E_n(X_{p,m}(R)) \le C_p R(n/\log m)^{1/2-1/p}$ is an asymptotic minimax-rate statement. A's Theorem 1.3 is an exact-recovery (zero-error) statement under deterministic conditions. Although B's Theorem 9 (which IS matched to A's Theorem 1.3) feeds into TP21.1, the rate-theorem itself is conceptually upstream of A and has no direct A analogue.
B's adaptive vs non-adaptive equivalence ($E_n \le 2^{1/p} E_n^{\mathrm{Adapt}}$) is purely a Donoho/IBC-style minimax statement. A does not consider adaptive sampling at all.
B's $E_n \asymp d^n$ equivalence is the Optimal-Recovery / approximation-theory bridge. A does not connect to $n$-widths.

B's near-optimality theorem combining the CS information operator + Basis Pursuit is a B-side packaging statement. A's Theorem 1.4 is the closest analogue in spirit but is an exact-recovery, not near-optimality, claim.

B's Theorem 7 ('near-optimality of widths under CS conditions') gives $w(\Phi, b_{p,m}) \le C(n/\log m)^{1/2-1/p}$. A has no width-bound analogue - A bounds RIP constants instead. The numerical conclusion (rate $(n/\log m)^{1/2-1/p}$) matches A's compressible-signal Theorem 5.1, but Theorem 7 itself is in width vocabulary.
B's alternative formulation (A1+A2 imply $\ell_1$ recovery rate) is a refactoring of B's main theorem in terms of $\nu$ and $w(\Phi,b_{1,m})$. No A counterpart at this level of abstraction.
B's Feasible-Point Lemma 3.1 ($\|x_0 - \hat x\|_2 \le 2 E_n$) bridges the minimax-error definition to the explicit reconstruction. A has no analogous step because A is not in the minimax framework.

B's nullspace concentration bound and $\ell_1$ stability lemma are the engine of B's $\ell_1$ recovery proof. A's proof uses dual certificates and does not have a $\nu$-stability lemma. Conceptually overlaps with A's PP2.4 strategy but expressed in disjoint technical vocabulary.
B's 'central algorithm' (Chebyshev-center reconstruction) is OR/IBC theory. A does not invoke this construction.

B's CS information operator $I_n^{\mathrm{CS}} = \Phi\Psi^T$ is the random-projection sampling architecture. A's coding matrix $A$ plays an analogous role at a high level but A treats $A$ as fixed Gaussian and never composes with a transform basis $\Psi$. The transform-domain composition is uniquely B's framing.

B's iterative kill-and-project algorithm constructs the dual certificate $y$. While A also constructs a dual certificate iteratively (in PP2.3), A's iteration is series/telescoping in $H$ and is not framed as a kill-and-project numerical algorithm. The conceptual analogy is captured by the LP2.4 / LP21.9-LP21.10 match; AP21.4 by itself as an algorithm has no A counterpart.

B's Basis-Pursuit near-optimality corollary in the case $p=1$ is a packaging statement specific to the minimax framing of B. A's CP2.1 (Gaussian decoding corollary) is an exact-recovery corollary, not a rate-equivalence one.
B's general $(P_p)$ least-norm reconstruction is a one-parameter family of which $(P_1)$ is the convex case. A only considers $p=1$, so the abstract $(P_p)$ family has no A counterpart.
